sources.title: UNESCO: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe
sources.note: Royal city, pyramids, Naqa and Musawwarat, reservoirs and wider cultural connections.

sources.title: Rilly and de Voogt: The Meroitic Language and Writing System, historical introduction
sources.note: Cambridge University Press excerpt: continuity from Napata, indigenous gods, fourth-century transformation and uncertainty about its causes.

sources.title: German Archaeological Institute: Hamadab
sources.note: Excavation project: public well, workshops, kitchens, utensils, urban plan and occupation sequence.

sources.title: Ulrike Nowotnick: Ceramic Technology, Production and Use in an Urban Settlement on the Middle Nile
sources.note: DAI 2022 monograph, synopsis and domestic pottery study; late Meroitic Hamadab, second to fourth centuries CE.

sources.title: Humphris and colleagues: Iron Smelting in Sudan
sources.note: 2018 experimental archaeology paper, archaeological smelting debris and experimental reconstruction of late and post-Meroitic workshops.

sources.title: Kozieradzka-Ogunmakin and Sołtysiak: Isotopic evidence of an environmental shift at the fall of Meroe
sources.note: Antiquity 97 (2023), pages 1501 to 1515. Thirteen cemeteries, changing climate and crops; environmental contribution is proposed, not a single established cause.

sources.title: Claude Rilly: New Light on the Royal Lineage in the Last Decades of the Meroitic Kingdom
sources.note: Sudan and Nubia 21 (2017), appendix pages 144 to 147. Line 2 of the Talakhidamani inscription gives qor; page 145 explains qorel > qor and ruler plus article. Direct fetch intermittent; source text checked through indexed PDF excerpts.

sources.title: Unicode Consortium: Meroitic Cursive character names
sources.note: Standard character mapping used for the normalized typed rendering: QA U+109B3, O U+109A3, RA U+109AB. This is not a facsimile.

sources.title: Scuola Normale Superiore: Funerary stele of Wiritelito
sources.note: Transcription and translation, including family relationships and offerings. The web caption mistakenly says BCE; the cited Soleb volume dates REM0289 to the second half of the third century CE.

sources.title: Histoire et civilisations du Soudan: Wiritelito stele REM0289
sources.note: Soleb 2017, printed page 367: Karanog, second half of third century CE. Corrects the Mnamon web caption date.

sources.title: Volubilis archaeological site: The pre-Roman city
sources.note: Pre-Roman wall, Punic inscriptions, magistrates, imported ceramics, coins and continuity after annexation.

sources.title: Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites: Lixus
sources.note: M. Euzennat, 1976. Early houses and temples; distinguish Mauretanian remains from later Roman industrial installations.

sources.title: Fantuzzi and colleagues: Petrographic characterization of Lixus amphorae
sources.note: Lucentum 45 (2026), samples from 2018 and 2021 excavations, late Mauretanian through late Roman dates; regional container imports, not all local manufacture.

sources.title: British Museum: Coin of Juba II and Cleopatra Selene
sources.note: Silver coin 1931,0303.2, 25 BCE to 24 CE; portraits of both rulers; purchased collection object rather than controlled excavation.

sources.title: Berlin Coin Cabinet: Juba II denarius of 11/12 CE
sources.note: Object 18237896: REX IVBA, lion skin, cornucopia and trident; struck at Caesarea, dated to regnal year 36. Later than the map endpoint and explicitly labelled.

sources.title: Duane Roller: Juba II of Mauretania
sources.note: Geographers of the Ancient Greek World, 2024. Greek literary production, earlier sources, geography and royal cultural policy.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Western North Africa, 1 to 500 CE
sources.note: Timeline: client kingdom 25 BCE to 40 CE; murder of Ptolemy and Roman incorporation.

sources.title: Averil Cameron: Vandal and Byzantine Africa
sources.note: Cambridge Ancient History chapter 20: kingdom, rural continuity, Albertini documents and 533/534 reconquest.

sources.title: Jonathan Conant: Languages and Communities in Late Antique and Early Medieval North Africa
sources.note: 2023 chapter, pages 37 to 57: Latin administration, multilingual regional society, Luxorius and cultural continuity.

sources.title: Philip de Souza: Rome and the Vandals
sources.note: 2017 chapter, merchant crews and mixed maritime occupations following the 439 conquest.

sources.title: Járrega: Late Roman pottery imports in eastern Hispania Tarraconensis
sources.note: Accepted manuscript, late fifth- and early sixth-century contexts at Tarragona and Can Modolell; maintenance and expansion of African ceramic trade.

sources.title: Marie Elizabeth Ann DeMarre: Factors which influenced autonomy and independence for women
sources.note: University of South Africa thesis; Albertini tablets 11, 27 and 33 on widows; wives participating in transactions under Roman law.

sources.title: Robin Whelan: African Controversy, the Inheritance of the Donatist Schism in Vandal Africa
sources.note: Homoian and Nicene churches, doctrinal difference, disputation and continuity; not a single unvarying policy of persecution.

sources.title: Berlin Coin Cabinet: Hilderic silver coin
sources.note: Object 18201518, struck at Carthage from 523 to 530; D N HILDI-RIX REX and FELIX-KARTG, personified Carthage.

sources.title: Austrian Academy of Sciences: Coinage of the Vandal Empire in North Africa
sources.note: Research project, coin dies and hoards for chronology, economic and political history.

sources.title: Jan Jansen: In Defense of Mali’s Gold
sources.note: Journal of West African History 1 (2015), pages 1 to 36. Argument for an organized Kangaba frontier between about 1650 and 1850, rather than a simple disappearance of Mali.

sources.title: UNESCO: Septennial re-roofing ceremony of the Kamablon
sources.note: Community nomination, inscribed 2009. Building attributed to 1653; present-day ceremony and intergenerational transmission. Text checked in search-indexed UNESCO copy when direct page challenged.

sources.title: Jan Jansen: When Marrying a Muslim
sources.note: Journal of African History 57 (2016), pages 25 to 45; author abstract reproduced by African Union library. Concerns stories about elite marriages, not a survey of every household.

sources.title: UNESCO: Manden Charter, proclaimed in Kurukan Fuga
sources.note: Living oral heritage and its social values. The card does not claim a surviving medieval manuscript or unchanged historical wording.

sources.title: Kathryn L. Green: Mande Kaba, the Capital of Mali: A Recent Invention?
sources.note: Historical critique of identifying Kangaba with the medieval imperial capital; distinguish later political importance from retrospective traditions.

sources.title: Institut de Recherche sur le Maghreb Contemporain: Taʾrikh al-Sudan
sources.note: Catalogue of the 1898 Arabic edition of al-Saʿdi’s seventeenth-century chronicle. Arabic title is attested; regional comparison, not a Kangaba government document.

sources.title: R. S. O’Fahey: Foreword to In Darfur
sources.note: NYU Press, historical framing: emergence about 1650, conquest 1874, restoration 1898 and British annexation 1916.

sources.title: Library of Arabic Literature: In Darfur, Volume Two
sources.note: Publisher description of al-Tunisi’s travels beginning in 1803, family reunion, estate management and illustrated account.

sources.title: Humphrey Davies: Crossing Cultures, a Nineteenth-Century Egyptian’s Story of Darfur
sources.note: Translator interview, 2018: multilingual court, Fur transcriptions, army title and the later composition of the account.

sources.title: Sudan’s Living Heritage Museum: Food and drink of the Fur
sources.note: Historical section discusses al-Tunisi’s early nineteenth-century food account. Modern health claims on the page are not used.

sources.title: O’Fahey and Abu Salim: Land in Dar Fur, Estate and privilege
sources.note: 1983 scholarly study of land charters and grants to chiefs, holy men, merchants and royal relatives; privileges involved rights over people, not simply modern freehold land.

sources.title: NYU Press: Arabic title of In Darfur
sources.note: Publisher-supplied bibliographic title تشحيذ الأذهان بسيرة بلاد العرب والسودان; brief Arabic excerpt, modern typed spelling, literal translation.

sources.title: D. N. Beach: The Mutapa Dynasty, a Comparison of Documentary and Traditional Evidence
sources.note: History in Africa 3 (1976), pages 1 to 17. Northern plateau and Zambezi geography; continuing dynastic fragments; critical comparison of sources.

sources.title: Pikirayi and Lindahl: Ceramics, Ethnohistory, and Ethnography
sources.note: African Archaeological Review 30 (2013), pages 455 to 473. Baranda/Massapa, local cooking pottery, burnishing tools and commercial exchange.

sources.title: Koleini, Pikirayi and Colomban: Revisiting Baranda
sources.note: Antiquity 91 (2017), pages 751 to 764. Chemical and structural analysis identifies a predominantly south Asian origin for the studied glass beads.

sources.title: Chirikure and Rehren: Iron Smelting in Pre-Colonial Zimbabwe
sources.note: Journal of African Archaeology 4 (2006), pages 37 to 54. Baranda dated about 1500 to 1700 contrasted with the earlier Swart Village assemblage.

sources.title: Ana Cristina Roque: Political power and Portuguese presence in sixteenth-century Sofala
sources.note: Anais de História de Além-Mar V (2004), pages 185 to 252, especially 187 to 189: Alcaçova’s account depended on Sofala informants and Portuguese political aims.

sources.title: Diogo de Alcaçova’s 1506 letter, in Theal’s Records of South-Eastern Africa I
sources.note: 1898 edition, Portuguese pages 57 to 62 and English translation pages 63 to 67. Brief original-language excerpt on page 58; translation page 64.

sources.title: Zimbabwe Field Guide: The decline of the Mutapa state, about 1623 to 1902
sources.note: Locally focused synthesis citing Mudenge, Beach, Pikirayi and Isaacman. Used for later political changes and attributed palace description; no claim that every ruler was always a Portuguese puppet.

sources.title: Machiridza and Kapumha: Beyond Colonial Boundaries
sources.note: Land 12 (2023), article 1625. Rozvi formation about 1685 to 1830, landscape memory, continuity across Torwa/Rozvi political change and oral narratives.

sources.title: Lesley Hatipone Machiridza: Landscapes and Ethnicity
sources.note: Historical Archaeology 54 (2020), pages 647 to 675. Danamombe, Naletale and Zinjanja excavation, detailed household finds and chronology.

sources.title: National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe: Naletale Cluster of Dzimbabwes
sources.note: Zimbabwe’s 2018 UNESCO Tentative List submission, not an inscribed World Heritage property. Named sites, wall patterns, mining remains and earlier antiquarian damage.

sources.title: Zimbabwe Field Guide: The Rozvi State
sources.note: Locally focused synthesis citing Mudenge, Beach and Mazarire. Used narrowly for farming, trade and nineteenth-century political breakup.

sources.title: Ahmet Kavas: Vedây, TDV Encyclopaedia of Islam
sources.note: 2012 scholarly entry, foundation, learning networks, trade and nineteenth-century diplomatic letter illustration. Exact printed Arabic name وداي is a modern reference spelling.

sources.title: Chad Ministry of Culture: Ruins of Ouara
sources.note: 2005 UNESCO Tentative List submission. Palace layout and mosque; not an inscribed World Heritage property. Its sixteenth-century palace attribution is not used because it conflicts with the better-supported dynastic chronology.

sources.title: Dennis D. Cordell: Eastern Libya, Wadai and the Sanusiya
sources.note: Journal of African History 18 (1977), pages 21 to 36. Route opening about 1809 or 1810; religious networks, trade security and dispute settlement.

sources.title: Al-Tunisi: Travels of an Arab Merchant in Soudan, Part II, Wadai
sources.note: Bayle St John’s 1854 English abridgement through a French version of the early nineteenth-century traveler’s account. Used as attributed observation, not universal custom or neutral racial description.

sources.title: Douglas E. Saxon: Wadai (Ouaddai) Empire
sources.note: Encyclopedia of Empire (2016), abstract: trans-Saharan trade, slavery and French defeat in 1909.

sources.title: French union manuscript catalogue: Dijon manuscript 3535
sources.note: Catalogue records a 260-leaf Arabic manuscript seized at Djoua, Wadai, in 1908. Identification as a Quran and nineteenth-century date both carry question marks.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Index 500 BCE to 500 CE; polygons in the Middle Nile, 29.5 to 36 east and 12.5 to 23.5 north. Narrative covers later Kush distinctly from existing kush card. Fourth-century political transformation is explicitly earlier than final imported 500 CE polygon. Original q-o-r is standardized Unicode from Rilly’s published reading, with separately cited character mapping.

Imported 200 BCE to 1 BCE polygons cover western Mauretania, roughly Morocco, not modern Mauritania. Card explicitly labels the first-century CE coin and annexation as later history. Existing Morocco narratives left unchanged.

Imported 500 to 600 polygon covers North Africa and Mediterranean islands. Known historical sovereignty ends in 534, not 600; retain the polygon without claiming correction. Card includes the earlier 439 establishment and explicit Byzantine phase afterward.

Index 1650 to 1783; polygon lies in southern Manding/Upper Niger, roughly 11.28 to 6.90 degrees west and 8.56 to 11.76 north. Existing mali-empire card remains separate. Jansen’s frontier reconstruction is explicitly attributed rather than treated as exact polygon sovereignty.

Index 1530 to 1815; geometry in western Sudan, about 22.69 to 30 east and 12.79 to 18.17 north. Earlier Tunjur/pre-Keira history is not silently recast as Keira sovereignty. Dates outside the imported interval are clearly later context.

Imported 1492 to 1650; polygons lie in Zimbabwe and Mozambique but the earliest outline extends far beyond the northern core described by Beach. Card does not validate every imported boundary. Portuguese sample is an external 1506 source, clearly labelled.

Imported 1650 to 1815; southwest Zimbabwe polygon about 26.28 to 30.69 east, 22.05 to 18 south. Earlier Torwa construction and later Rozvi occupation are distinguished. Modern recorded varozvi is explicitly not a seventeenth-century written inscription.

Imported 1530 to 1900, with a geometry gap between 1815 and 1878; polygons are in eastern Chad and adjoining borderlands. Seventeenth-century dynasty and 1909 conquest are separated from imported endpoints. Arabic sample is honestly labelled a modern printed name; illustrated historic letter is identified but not transcribed without readable access.
